rounds.q: Which small bean-shaped structures filter lymph and swell up during infections?
rounds.why: You have hundreds of them. Swollen neck nodes usually just mean your immune system is busy, which is exactly its job.

rounds.q: Red cells, white cells and platelets are mostly made in the?
rounds.why: Red marrow makes billions of new blood cells every day. In adults it’s mostly in flat bones like the pelvis, sternum and skull.

rounds.q: Which white blood cells does HIV mainly target?
rounds.why: CD4 helper T cells coordinate the immune response. With effective treatment today, most people living with HIV can expect a near-normal lifespan.

rounds.q: Where do T cells, the cells HIV targets, finish maturing?
rounds.why: T for thymus. HIV infects CD4 helper T cells; treatment now keeps the count up and the virus undetectable. Today is World AIDS Day.

rounds.q: What’s one of the highlighted organ’s main jobs?
rounds.why: The spleen recycles worn-out red cells and stores immune cells. You can live without one, but you’ll need some extra vaccines.

rounds.q: Name the highlighted part of the bowel.
rounds.why: An S-shaped loop on a mobile mesentery, which is why it can twist (volvulus).

rounds.q: Name the highlighted vessels.
rounds.why: The veins that carry oxygenated blood: from lungs to left atrium. Usually four of them.

rounds.q: Name the highlighted layer.
rounds.why: The tough white of the eye. It’s continuous with the clear cornea at the front.

rounds.q: Roughly how much blood does the highlighted chamber push out with each beat at rest?
rounds.why: Stroke volume is usually 60–100 mL; at around 70 beats a minute that’s about 5 litres a minute. Barney Clark lived 112 days on the Jarvik-7 artificial heart from 2 December 1982.

rounds.q: Name the highlighted airway.
rounds.why: Wider, shorter and more vertical than the left, so inhaled peanuts usually go right.

rounds.q: Name the highlighted cartilage.
rounds.why: More mobile and more circular than the medial meniscus, so it’s injured less often.

rounds.q: In adults, the spinal cord itself usually ends at about which vertebral level?
rounds.why: Below that, nerve roots run on as the cauda equina, which is why lumbar punctures go lower. Today is International Day of Persons with Disabilities.

rounds.q: A cochlear implant works by electrically stimulating which nerve?
rounds.why: It bypasses damaged hair cells and talks straight to the cochlear nerve. Graeme Clark’s team in Melbourne fitted their first multichannel implant in 1978.

rounds.q: Name the highlighted tube.
rounds.why: It equalises middle ear pressure. Shorter and flatter in children, which is one reason they get more ear infections.

rounds.q: Name the highlighted layer.
rounds.why: A blood-rich layer feeding the outer retina. Its pigment helps absorb stray light.

rounds.q: Name the highlighted vertebra.
rounds.why: No body and no spinous process. It holds up the skull, like the Titan Atlas.

rounds.q: Which nerve supplies pronator teres?
rounds.why: The median nerve usually passes between its two heads, a spot where it can be compressed.

rounds.q: Which nerve runs through Guyon’s canal at the wrist?
rounds.why: Cyclists can compress it from leaning on handlebars: ‘handlebar palsy’.

rounds.q: Name the highlighted bone.
rounds.why: The longest metacarpal, with the most rigid joint at its base. A stable post for pinching.

rounds.q: Name the highlighted vessel.
rounds.why: The largest vein in the body, carrying blood from the legs and abdomen.

rounds.q: Name the highlighted ossicle.
rounds.why: The ‘hammer’, attached to the eardrum. You can often see its handle through an otoscope.

rounds.q: Tetanus causes ‘lockjaw’. Spasm of which muscle clamps the jaw shut?
rounds.why: Tetanus spores live in soil. The toxin blocks the nerve signals that tell muscles to relax, and the powerful masseter is often first to clamp. Today is World Soil Day: keep that booster current.

rounds.q: Name the highlighted valve.
rounds.why: The outflow valve of the right ventricle. The least likely of the four to cause trouble in adults.

rounds.q: Which nerve supplies the skin of the first web space on the top of the foot?
rounds.why: Its only skin patch. Numbness here can be an early sign of anterior compartment syndrome.

rounds.q: Name the highlighted bone.
rounds.answer: Middle phalanx of the middle finger
wrong: Proximal phalanx of the middle finger
Distal phalanx of the middle finger
rounds.why: Each finger has three phalanges: proximal, middle and distal. The thumb has only two.

rounds.q: Name the highlighted vertebra.
rounds.why: The first thoracic vertebra, carrying the first rib. Count down from C1 at the top.

rounds.q: Which nerve supplies popliteus?
rounds.why: Popliteus ‘unlocks’ the fully straightened knee, allowing it to bend.

rounds.q: Which artery runs in the groove over the front of the highlighted wall and causes the ‘widow-maker’ heart attack?
rounds.why: The LAD feeds the front wall and most of the septum. Finland’s North Karelia Project, begun in 1972, cut heart disease deaths dramatically by changing a whole region’s diet and smoking habits.

rounds.q: Which vein drains most of the heart’s own blood into the right atrium?
rounds.why: It runs in the back of the atrioventricular groove. Leads for cardiac resynchronisation pacing are threaded through it to reach the left ventricle.

rounds.q: Which nerve supplies adductor pollicis?
rounds.why: Weak adductor pollicis makes you bend the thumb tip to grip paper: Froment’s sign.

rounds.q: Yawning on a plane opens the highlighted tube. What does it connect the middle ear to?
rounds.why: The Eustachian tube equalises pressure. A blocked one on descent is why flying with a cold makes your ears ache.

rounds.q: Calf exercises on long flights help pump blood up the leg veins. Which muscle makes most of the calf bulge?
rounds.why: Every squeeze pushes blood back towards the heart through one-way valves. Flex your ankles and walk the aisle on long-haul.

rounds.q: Which gland releases melatonin, the ‘time for bed’ hormone that jet lag throws out?
rounds.why: A pea-sized gland deep in the brain that releases melatonin when it gets dark. Descartes thought it was the seat of the soul.

rounds.q: Which blood vessels have walls just one cell thick, for swapping oxygen with tissues?
rounds.why: They’re so narrow that red blood cells squeeze through in single file.

rounds.q: Which part of you senses movement and tilt, and makes you queasy when it disagrees with your eyes?
rounds.why: The vestibular system in the inner ear says ‘we’re moving’, your eyes say ‘still cabin’, and your brain responds with motion sickness.

rounds.q: What’s the body’s largest organ?
rounds.why: Around 2 square metres in an adult. The liver is the largest internal organ.

rounds.q: How many bones are in one adult hand, wrist included?
rounds.why: 8 carpals, 5 metacarpals and 14 phalanges. Your two hands hold over a quarter of your 206 bones.

rounds.q: What’s the hardest substance in the human body?
rounds.why: Tooth enamel is about 96% mineral. It can’t regrow, so be nice to it.

rounds.q: What does the highlighted structure do?
rounds.answer: Controls how much light gets in
rounds.why: The iris is a ring of muscle that widens or narrows the pupil. Its pattern is so individual that it’s used in ID scanners.

rounds.q: Which tendon joins the calf muscles to the heel?
rounds.why: The body’s thickest, strongest tendon, named after the Greek hero who was held by the heel when dipped in the river Styx.

rounds.q: Name the highlighted wrist bone.
rounds.why: Pea-sized and sitting on the front of the triquetrum. It’s a sesamoid bone inside a tendon.

rounds.q: Which muscle is the usual site for an adult’s vaccine?
rounds.why: Aim for the meaty part a few finger-breadths below the bony tip of the shoulder. Too high risks a painful shoulder injury.

rounds.q: Name the highlighted pouch.
rounds.why: The first part of the large bowel. The appendix hangs from it.

rounds.q: Which cranial nerve moves the tongue?
rounds.why: Damage it and the tongue points towards the weak side when you stick it out.

rounds.q: Name the highlighted bone.
rounds.why: The palm bone behind the middle finger. It’s the only metacarpal with a little styloid process at its base.

rounds.q: Perth’s Barry Marshall drank a culture of the bug that lives in the highlighted organ to prove it causes gastritis. Which bug?
rounds.why: Marshall and Robin Warren won the 2005 Nobel Prize. The stomach was meant to be too acidic for bacteria; H. pylori disagreed.

rounds.q: ‘Place cells’, part of the brain’s GPS (2014 Nobel), were found in which structure?
rounds.why: John O’Keefe found place cells there in 1971; May-Britt and Edvard Moser later found grid cells next door in the entorhinal cortex.

rounds.q: Melbourne-born John Eccles won a 1963 Nobel for how nerve cells signal each other. What’s the gap between two neurons called?
rounds.why: Signals usually cross it as chemical messengers. Eccles shared the prize with Alan Hodgkin and Andrew Huxley.

rounds.q: Hubel and Wiesel won a 1981 Nobel for showing how cells in the highlighted area respond to edges and lines. Which cortex?
rounds.why: They found neurons that fire for lines at particular angles, the building blocks of how we see shapes.

rounds.q: Santiago Ramón y Cajal shared the 1906 Nobel Prize for showing the nervous system is built from?
rounds.why: He shared it with Camillo Golgi, whose silver stain he used and who still backed the ‘continuous net’ idea. Today is Nobel Prize Day.

rounds.q: Low oxygen at altitude makes lung arteries constrict. What’s this called?
rounds.why: Handy for diverting blood from poorly aired patches of lung, but at altitude it squeezes the whole lot, raising pressure and paving the way for HAPE.

rounds.q: At altitude, the kidney pumps out more erythropoietin. Which cells make it?
rounds.answer: Peritubular interstitial cells of the cortex
rounds.why: They sense low oxygen, and EPO rises within hours of arriving up high. The extra red cells take weeks to build up. Juxtaglomerular cells make renin. Today is International Mountain Day.

rounds.q: Which sensors in the neck detect low oxygen and drive faster breathing at altitude?
rounds.why: Tiny clusters at the carotid fork with a huge blood flow for their size. The central chemoreceptors mostly track carbon dioxide, not oxygen.

rounds.q: The highlighted point is where the trachea splits. At about which vertebral level is it?
rounds.why: Level with the sternal angle. An endotracheal tube tip should sit a few centimetres above it.

rounds.q: Severe brain swelling, as in high-altitude cerebral oedema, can push the brainstem through which opening?
rounds.why: Herniation through the foramen magnum squashes the brainstem’s breathing centres. That’s why HACE means going down, fast.

rounds.q: After a mosquito bite, malaria parasites first multiply in which cells?
rounds.why: They hide in the liver for about a week before bursting out into red cells. The RTS,S vaccine, piloted for young children in Kenya, Ghana and Malawi from 2019, targets that early stage.

rounds.q: In malaria the highlighted organ can swell hugely. Which way does it grow?
rounds.answer: Down towards the right iliac fossa
wrong: Back towards the left kidney only
rounds.why: It grows down and across the abdomen, with a notch you can sometimes feel. You can’t get your hand above it, which helps tell it from a big kidney.

rounds.q: Which nerve is at risk in thyroid surgery and can leave a hoarse voice?
rounds.why: It runs up beside the thyroid to supply most of the voice box muscles. The left one loops under the aortic arch on the way.

rounds.q: Which nerve supplies supraspinatus and infraspinatus?
rounds.why: It can get trapped at the suprascapular or spinoglenoid notch. Volleyball players are known for wasting of infraspinatus from it.

rounds.q: Name the highlighted bone.
rounds.answer: Distal phalanx of the little finger
wrong: Middle phalanx of the little finger
Distal phalanx of the ring finger
rounds.why: Fingertip bones end in a rough tuft that supports the pulp. They’re the most commonly broken bones in the hand, usually from crush injuries.

rounds.q: The sinoatrial node sits at the top of which groove on the outside of the right atrium?
rounds.why: The sulcus terminalis outside matches the crista terminalis inside. In 1947 Claude Beck reported shocking a stopped heart back to life during surgery.

rounds.q: The moderator band in the right ventricle carries which part of the conduction system?
rounds.why: The septomarginal trabecula is a shortcut to the anterior papillary muscle, so it tightens in time with the rest of the ventricle.

rounds.q: Which pericardial space can a surgeon pass a finger through, behind the aorta and pulmonary trunk?
rounds.why: Cardiac surgeons use it to get a clamp or tape around the great arteries. The oblique sinus, behind the left atrium, is a dead end.

rounds.q: Which nerve supplies geniohyoid?
rounds.answer: C1 fibres travelling with the hypoglossal
rounds.why: The hypoglossal is just the bus. The passengers are C1 spinal nerve fibres.

rounds.q: Which nerve supplies flexor pollicis longus?
wrong: Median nerve proper, in the palm
rounds.why: Lose it and you can’t make an ‘OK’ sign: the thumb and index tips go flat.

rounds.q: About how much blood does an average adult have?
rounds.why: Roughly 7% of body weight. Over about 12 hours in 1799, George Washington’s doctors removed around 2.4 litres, some 40% of his blood. He died that night.

rounds.q: Which vessels carry blood back to the heart?
rounds.why: Bloodletting usually opened an arm vein at the inner elbow, the same spot used for blood tests today.

rounds.q: Which flap covers the entrance to the larynx when you swallow?
rounds.why: George Washington probably died of acute epiglottitis on this day in 1799, after his doctors drained a large share of his blood.

rounds.q: Where does the highlighted chamber pump its blood?
rounds.why: The right ventricle sends blood on a short, low-pressure trip to the lungs, so its wall is much thinner than the left’s.

rounds.q: Which paired lumps of immune tissue sit either side of the back of the throat?
rounds.why: Part of a ring of immune tissue guarding the entrance to your airway and gut. Removing them was once almost a childhood rite of passage.

rounds.q: What does the highlighted structure do?
wrong: Controls how much light gets in
rounds.why: The cornea does most of the bending; the lens adjusts for near or far. L. L. Zamenhof, born today in 1859, was an eye doctor who also invented Esperanto.

rounds.q: What’s the black opening in the middle of the iris called?
rounds.why: It’s not a thing, it’s a hole. It looks black because the light that goes in mostly doesn’t come back out.

rounds.q: Which cells in the retina let you see colour?
rounds.why: About 6 million cones handle colour and detail; around 120 million rods take the night shift in black and white.

rounds.q: Which gland makes your tears?
rounds.why: It sits above the outer corner of each eye. Tears drain through tiny holes in the inner corner into your nose, which is why crying makes it run.

rounds.q: Where the optic nerve leaves the eye there are no light sensors. What’s that spot called?
rounds.why: Each eye has one, but your brain fills the gap so neatly that you never notice.

rounds.q: What do the highlighted tiny bones do?
rounds.why: The ossicles work as a lever, boosting pressure about 20-fold so sound can move the fluid of the inner ear. Beethoven, born around today in 1770, lost his hearing gradually from his late twenties.

rounds.q: Which structure in the cochlea turns sound vibrations into nerve signals?
rounds.why: Its hair cells are where most noise and age-related hearing loss starts. Beethoven, born around this day in 1770, wrote his Ninth Symphony while profoundly deaf.

rounds.q: Which muscle, the body’s smallest, steadies the stapes to dampen loud sounds?
rounds.why: About a millimetre long and supplied by the facial nerve. Bell’s palsy can knock it out and make everyday sounds painfully loud.

rounds.q: What’s the medical name for earwax?
rounds.why: Made by glands in the outer ear canal. The canal skin slowly migrates outwards and cleans itself, so cotton buds mostly just push wax in.

rounds.q: Beethoven reportedly gripped a rod touching his piano in his teeth to hear. What did that use?
rounds.why: Vibrations travel through the skull straight to the cochlea, skipping the middle ear. It’s the idea behind the Rinne test and bone-anchored hearing aids.

rounds.q: Your master body clock, scrambled by jet lag, sits in which tiny part of the hypothalamus?
rounds.why: It sits just above the optic chiasm and resets from light reaching your eyes. Morning sunlight is the best jet lag cure.

rounds.q: Which deep vein behind the knee is a common site for DVT?
rounds.why: It drains the calf, and clots here can travel to the lungs. On long flights, flex your ankles and walk the aisle. The Wright brothers flew 12 seconds on this day in 1903, so no DVT risk for them.

rounds.q: Which sinuses most often cause pain from pressure change on a plane’s descent?
rounds.why: Their long, narrow drainage duct blocks easily when you have a cold. The Wright brothers first flew on this day in 1903.

rounds.q: Name the highlighted vertebra.
rounds.why: Its tooth-like dens is the pivot the atlas turns on when you shake your head ‘no’.

rounds.q: If cabin pressure drops, masks fall. In which tiny air sacs does the oxygen cross into blood?
rounds.why: Hundreds of millions of them, with a combined surface of around 70 square metres.

rounds.q: Reactivated tuberculosis classically affects which part of the lungs?
rounds.why: The apices are oxygen-rich with poorer lymph drainage, which suits TB. Many countries offer screening for latent TB to new arrivals; it’s very treatable.

rounds.q: Which nerve supplies fibularis (peroneus) longus and brevis, the foot’s evertors?
rounds.why: It also supplies most of the skin on top of the foot. The deep branch just gets the first web space.

rounds.q: Which nerve supplies the pelvic floor and the skin of the perineum?
rounds.why: From S2–4 (‘keeps the poo off the floor’). It’s the target of a pudendal block in childbirth.

rounds.q: Name the highlighted vertebra.
rounds.why: Count down from the top of the thoracic curve. The T4–T5 level lines up with the sternal angle, where the trachea splits.

rounds.q: A fixed, dilated pupil with the eye turned ‘down and out’ points to which nerve?
rounds.why: It moves most eye muscles and carries pupil-constricting fibres on its outside, so pressure from an aneurysm blows the pupil early.

rounds.q: Rickets widens and frays which part of a child’s long bone?
rounds.why: The growth plate sits between epiphysis and metaphysis. Low vitamin D lets it widen, a key X-ray sign. Rickets is one of the many guesses at Tiny Tim’s illness.

rounds.q: Which tiny glands behind the thyroid control blood calcium?
rounds.why: Usually four, each about the size of a grain of rice. They’re easy to remove by accident in thyroid surgery.

rounds.q: Which is the body’s strongest ligament, across the front of the hip?
rounds.why: The Y ligament of Bigelow stops the hip bending backwards, so you can stand upright with little muscle effort.

rounds.q: A blow to the outside of the knee tears the highlighted ligament. What’s the classic ‘unhappy triad’?
rounds.why: Described by O’Donoghue in 1950. The MCL is attached to the medial meniscus, though lateral meniscus tears turn out to be common in these injuries too.

rounds.q: Rickets classically causes knobbly swellings where the ribs meet their cartilage, called the?
rounds.why: Too little vitamin D, so bone doesn’t mineralise. One theory for Tiny Tim in A Christmas Carol, published on this day in 1843, is rickets with tuberculosis.

rounds.q: Which nerve supplies cricothyroid, the one voice box muscle the recurrent laryngeal nerve doesn’t?
rounds.why: Cricothyroid tightens the vocal cords for high notes. Damage it in thyroid surgery and your voice can lose its top end.

rounds.q: Besides the aorta, what else passes through the aortic hiatus of the diaphragm?
rounds.why: ‘I ate 10 eggs at 12’: IVC at T8, oesophagus at T10, aorta at T12, with the thoracic duct (and often the azygos vein) tagging along.

rounds.q: Which muscle is the only abductor of the vocal cords?
rounds.why: Lose both and the cords can’t open, which threatens the airway.

rounds.q: Which tendon forms the ulnar (inner) border of the anatomical snuffbox?
rounds.why: EPB and APL form the other side. EPL hooks around Lister’s tubercle and can snap weeks after a wrist fracture.

rounds.q: Arnold’s nerve, supplying part of the ear canal, is a branch of which nerve?
rounds.why: Its auricular branch. That’s why cleaning some people’s ears makes them cough.

rounds.q: What does the highlighted ligament mainly stop?
rounds.why: The ACL stops the tibia shooting forward under the femur. Awkward landings from a jump tear it, which is why basketballers dread it. Today is World Basketball Day.

rounds.q: A typical rolled ankle injures ligaments on which side?
rounds.why: Rolling the foot inwards stretches the outer ligaments, most often the anterior talofibular. It’s one of basketball’s commonest injuries.

rounds.q: Stress hormones like adrenaline come from glands sitting on top of which organs?
rounds.why: The adrenal glands sit on the kidneys like little hats. Slow breathing and meditation can help dial the stress response down. Today is World Meditation Day.

rounds.q: Which muscle bends the elbow and also turns a screwdriver or doorknob palm-up?
rounds.why: Biceps is a powerful twister (supinator) as well as a flexor. The real workhorse for bending the elbow, brachialis, hides underneath.

rounds.q: How many vertebrae are in the human neck?
rounds.why: Seven, the same as a giraffe. Theirs are just much longer.

rounds.q: What does the highlighted organ do?
rounds.why: The liver makes bile and the gallbladder stores it, squeezing it out after a fatty meal. You can live fine without one.

rounds.q: The liver sits mostly in which part of the abdomen?
rounds.why: Tucked under the right ribs. Srinivasa Ramanujan, born today in 1887, probably died of a parasitic liver infection at just 32.

rounds.q: What are the tiny finger-like projections lining the small intestine called?
rounds.why: They hugely increase the surface for absorbing food. Coeliac disease flattens them.

rounds.q: How many teeth are in a full adult set?
rounds.why: 32 including the four wisdom teeth, which many people never fully get. Children have 20.

rounds.q: An amoebic liver abscess most often forms in which part of the liver?
rounds.why: The right lobe is bigger and gets most of the portal blood from the gut. Mathematician Srinivasa Ramanujan, born today in 1887, probably died of one.

rounds.q: Which gland sits on top of each kidney?
rounds.why: ‘Ad-renal’ just means next to the kidney. It makes adrenaline and cortisol.

rounds.q: What’s the kidney’s basic filtering unit called?
rounds.why: Each kidney has around a million. Joseph Murray’s 1954 transplant in Boston worked because donor and recipient were identical twins, so no rejection.

rounds.q: Which kidney usually sits lower, and why?
rounds.answer: Right, pushed down by the liver
wrong: Left, pushed down by the spleen
Right, pushed down by the heart
rounds.why: The bulky liver nudges the right kidney a little lower than the left.

rounds.q: Where is a transplanted kidney usually placed?
rounds.why: The native kidneys usually stay put. Joseph Murray did the first successful kidney transplant, between identical twins, on this day in 1954.

rounds.q: Blood reaches each kidney for filtering through which vessel?
rounds.why: The kidneys get around a fifth of the heart’s output, a huge share for organs the size of a fist.

rounds.q: Name the highlighted part of the bowel.
rounds.why: You’re facing the patient, so their right is on your left. It carries the post-feast leftovers up from the caecum.

rounds.q: Which enzyme, from the salivary glands and pancreas, starts digesting the Christmas potatoes?
rounds.why: Chew bread long enough and it starts to taste sweet: that’s amylase turning starch into sugar.

rounds.q: Fat from a feast is absorbed into lymph vessels in the gut lining called?
rounds.why: They turn milky white after a fatty meal, hence the name. The fat skips the liver at first and enters the blood via the thoracic duct.

rounds.q: Which part of the brain acts as the body’s thermostat?
rounds.why: It balances heat made (including from your Christmas lunch) against heat lost through skin and sweat. James Joule was born today in 1818.

rounds.q: Which ring of muscle stops stomach contents coming back up (when it behaves)?
rounds.why: Helped by the diaphragm. Big meals and lying down straight after Christmas lunch make heartburn more likely.

rounds.q: A tourniquet high on the thigh is there to compress which artery?
rounds.why: High and tight stops femoral bleeding. Clara Barton, born on Christmas Day 1821, nursed wounded soldiers before founding the American Red Cross.

rounds.q: Which artery is most often torn in an extradural haematoma?
rounds.why: It runs under the pterion, the thin spot at the side of the skull. Classic story: a knock, a lucid spell, then rapid decline.

rounds.q: Which nerve supplies the skin of the inner (medial) forearm?
rounds.why: It comes straight off the medial cord. The outer side belongs to the musculocutaneous nerve, via its lateral antebrachial cutaneous branch.

rounds.q: Name the highlighted vertebra.
rounds.why: A line across the tops of the iliac crests (Tuffier’s line) crosses about L4, the landmark for a lumbar puncture.

rounds.q: In most people, which artery supplies the sinoatrial node?
rounds.why: The RCA does it in a bit over half of people; the circumflex covers most of the rest.

rounds.q: Which cells build new bone, the place radium gets locked into?
rounds.why: Osteoblasts build, osteoclasts break down. Radium behaves like calcium, so it’s built into bone and irradiates it from inside. The Curies announced radium on this day in 1898.

rounds.q: Potassium iodide tablets are stockpiled for nuclear accidents to protect which gland?
rounds.why: The thyroid hoards iodine to make hormones. Flooding it with ordinary iodide stops it soaking up the radioactive kind.

rounds.q: Radium, announced by the Curies on this day in 1898, builds up in bone because the body treats it like?
rounds.why: Same column of the periodic table. The ‘Radium Girls’ who licked their brushes to paint watch dials developed jaw necrosis and bone cancers.

rounds.q: Name the highlighted bone.
rounds.answer: Middle phalanx of the index finger
wrong: Proximal phalanx of the index finger
Middle phalanx of the middle finger
Distal phalanx of the index finger
rounds.why: Every finger has three phalanges, the thumb just two. Marie Curie’s fingertips were left scarred and cracked from years of handling radium.

rounds.q: Which nerves carry ‘shoulder tip pain’ when the diaphragm is irritated?
rounds.why: They share the C3–4 roots with the phrenic nerve, so the brain blames the shoulder for the diaphragm’s problem.

rounds.q: Which muscle mainly opens the Eustachian tube when you swallow?
rounds.why: Unlike most palate muscles it’s supplied by V3, not the vagus. Young children’s shorter, flatter tubes help explain all those ear infections.

rounds.q: Which nerve supplies the parotid gland’s secretions?
rounds.why: Via the lesser petrosal nerve and otic ganglion, then hitching a ride on the auriculotemporal nerve. The facial nerve just runs through the gland.

rounds.q: Rabies virus reaches the brain from a bite by?
wrong: Crossing the skin to the spine
rounds.why: Retrograde axonal transport, which is why bites near the head have a shorter incubation. Louis Pasteur, born today in 1822, made the first rabies vaccine.

rounds.q: Ablation for atrial fibrillation often isolates the highlighted vessels. How many usually enter the left atrium?
rounds.why: Two from each lung, though three or five is a common variant. Muscle sleeves around their openings spark most AF.

rounds.q: Which of these does NOT pass through the carpal tunnel?
rounds.why: Nine tendons and the median nerve go through. Palmaris longus runs over the top, and about 1 in 7 people don’t have one at all.

rounds.q: What’s the biggest muscle in the body?
rounds.why: Your buttock muscle, the powerhouse for climbing stairs and standing up. A superhero muscle, just less photogenic.

rounds.q: What’s the outer layer of the skin called?
rounds.why: You shed millions of skin cells a day and renew the whole outer layer every month or two. Real-life regeneration.

rounds.q: Gigantism is usually caused by a growth-hormone tumour in which gland?
rounds.why: If it starts before the growth plates close you get gigantism; after, acromegaly. Comic writer Stan Lee was born today in 1922.

rounds.q: What does the highlighted structure mainly help with?
rounds.why: The cerebellum fine-tunes movement. Alcohol upsets it early, which is why police ask people to walk a straight line.

rounds.q: Radioactive spiders won’t help, but bones do repair themselves. A healing fracture forms a?
rounds.why: A soft callus of cartilage hardens into bone over weeks. Bone is one of the few tissues that can heal without a scar.

rounds.q: A urinary catheter passes up which tube to drain the bladder?
rounds.why: The urethra carries urine out. Rubber made catheters flexible, thanks to vulcanisation by Charles Goodyear, born today in 1800.

rounds.q: Which tubes carry urine from the kidneys to the bladder?
rounds.why: About 25–30 cm long. Urine is pushed along by squeezing waves, not just gravity, so you could wee upside down.

rounds.q: What connects muscle to bone?
rounds.why: Tendons pull, ligaments hold bone to bone. Both are springy, but nowhere near as stretchy as rubber.

rounds.q: What kind of blood fills the highlighted chamber?
rounds.why: The left atrium collects freshly oxygenated blood from the pulmonary veins and passes it to the left ventricle.

rounds.q: What’s the bendy tissue that shapes your nose and outer ear?
rounds.why: Flexible, a bit like rubber, but with no blood vessels of its own, which is why it heals so slowly.

rounds.q: Name the highlighted vertebra. Count carefully.
rounds.why: The last thoracic vertebra, carrying the floating 12th rib. Counting up from L5 is quickest.

rounds.q: A ligament of Struthers, when present, can trap which nerve above the elbow?
rounds.why: Not to be confused with the arcade of Struthers, which can catch the ulnar nerve. Struthers liked naming things.

rounds.q: What is the sesamoid bone sometimes found in the lateral head of gastrocnemius?
rounds.why: Present in about a third of people. Once thought to be vanishing, it’s become more common over the past century.

rounds.q: Shingles vesicles on the tip of the nose (Hutchinson’s sign) mean which nerve is involved?
rounds.why: It’s the end of the nasociliary branch of V1, which also supplies the eye. Hence the warning sign for eye involvement.

rounds.q: Palatoglossus is the one tongue muscle the hypoglossal doesn’t supply. What does?
rounds.why: It’s really a palate muscle moonlighting in the tongue, so it follows the palate’s nerve supply: the vagus.

rounds.q: Alcohol makes you wee more by blocking which hormone?
rounds.why: ADH from the posterior pituitary tells the kidneys to hold onto water. Block it and you lose more than you drink. Hello, New Year’s Day headache.

rounds.q: Boerhaave syndrome, a burst oesophagus after forceful vomiting, usually tears which part?
rounds.answer: Left side of the lower oesophagus
wrong: Right side of the upper oesophagus
rounds.why: The lower left wall is the weakest. Herman Boerhaave, born today in 1668, described it in a Dutch admiral after a feast.

rounds.q: Which skin layer holds the nerve endings, sweat glands and hair roots that deep burns destroy?
rounds.why: Burns deep enough to destroy the dermis’s nerve endings can hurt less than shallow ones. Enjoy the fireworks from a safe distance tonight.

rounds.q: Name the highlighted bone.
rounds.why: The thumb has only two phalanges; the fingers have three. Hands are the body part most often hurt by fireworks, so keep yours away from the fuse.

rounds.q: Which brain region’s ‘brakes’ does alcohol loosen early, so you dance like nobody’s watching?
rounds.why: The prefrontal cortex handles judgement and restraint. Coordination goes next, and at very high doses the brainstem’s breathing centres. Pace yourself tonight.
